newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Catholic puts new peace ideas to British PM.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Catholic puts new peace ideas to British PM.

text.p: A Northern Ireland Catholic leader said on Friday he had put fresh peace ideas to British Prime Minister John Major which he was sure could work despite an Irish nationalist bomb attempt on a police base.

"I have fully briefed (Prime Minister) John Major and his government and I now know that peace can be restored to our streets. I hope it will happen sooner rather than later," SDLP party chief John Hume said.
Twenty-four hours after renegade Irish republicans tried to blow up a police base here, Hume said he was convinced his proposals could bring an end to guerrilla violence.

Hume said the ideas arose from meetings he had had with Gerry Adams, leader of Sinn Fein, the political arm of the outlawed Irish Republican Army, the chief guerrilla force fighting to ending Britain's rule in the province.
"I am awaiting (a reply) with hope. I know that peace in Northern Ireland has been at the top of the Prime Minister's agenda.," he said in an interview with Reuters.
"I certainly hope that in the near future he will clarify clearly in a manner that will lead to a total restoration of the (IRA) ceasefire."
Hume declined to detail the ideas he has put to Major, but said: "I believe very strongly from my dialogue with Gerry Adams that that ceasefire can be restored."
Britain, backed by Ireland, says the IRA must reinstate a truce it ended in February for Sinn Fein to be admitted to all-party talks on the future of the British-ruled province.

Sinn Fein has signalled the IRA will not call a peace unless Britain promises it an unconditional place in "meaningful negotations" that are not stymied by demands by the province's pro-British parties for an early surrender of guerrilla weapons.
The IRA abandoned a 17-month ceasefire accusing Britain of reneging on a pledge of a Sinn Fein seat in talks.

The IRA has not struck since October 7 when it bombed British military headquarters south of Belfast. But a maverick group, the Irish Continuity Army Council, targetted Londonderry's police base with a 600 pounds (275 kilo) car bomb on Thursday.
The device was defused after the group telephoned a warning. Political analysts say the incident was a bid to destroy slender hopes of a peace deal.
Hume's party represents the bulk of Catholics in Northern Ireland, who account for 40 per cent of the population, and most of whom want a peaceful transition to an all-Ireland state.
Major has already said that it will take more than soft words from the IRA to convince a suspicious British public that a new guerrilla truce is meant to last.
Hume said the original September 1994 IRA truce, which he helped to broker, had broken down because of republicans' distrust of Britain.

He said his new propositions did not involve Britain making political concessions and were geared towards providing "reassurance" about the nature of all-party talks and the comprehensive nature of a talks agenda.

"When I say that we have a real opportunity to achieve a total ending of violence, I am not talking lightly. I am talking very very seriously and I am willing to put my political reputation on the line behind that statement," he said.
